# Scale benchmark (generated by `python -m pipeline.bench`)

1000 tickets arriving at once, worked by 3 sessions in parallel (one schema each, like separate banks), against 4,487,133 AMLworld transactions. Ran 2026-10-28 20:42:20 on Windows 11, AMD64, 16 logical CPUs, Python 3.14.3; Exasol 2026.2.0-nano.3.

## The golden hour

**1000 of 1000 tickets were worked within an hour of all arriving together.** Median time to hold 16.0 min, 95th percentile 31.4 min, last ticket 33.0 min. 30.3 tickets a minute.

One ticket's own work: median 5.60 s, 95th percentile 6.54 s, slowest 2.0 min.

## Time per step

| Step | Median | 95th percentile | Slowest |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| intake | 0.41 s | 0.53 s | 0.71 s |
| trace | 0.65 s | 0.84 s | 1.06 s |
| attribute | 1.17 s | 1.45 s | 1.77 s |
| score | 1.81 s | 2.29 s | 3.02 s |
| rules | 0.73 s | 0.92 s | 1.10 s |
| checks | 0.42 s | 0.54 s | 0.77 s |
| holds | 0.38 s | 0.49 s | 1.9 min |

## What happened to the tickets

- Worked to the end: 1000; with at least one hold: 959 (Rs 79,023,684,587 held in all).
- Intake found no exact match (nothing held, as at a bank): 0.
- Checks failed (nothing held automatically): 0.
- Stopped by an error: 0.

Each complaint reaches the bank 30 minutes after the payment, so the trace follows what had moved by then; money that moves later is the watch's job, as at a bank. Every ticket counts as arriving at the same moment, so the time to hold includes the wait in the queue: the worst case of a night when many complaints land together. In the lab schemas one bank owns every AMLworld account, so each trace follows every hop: more work than a bank that sees only its own. A laptop, not a bank's servers: the numbers are a floor to improve on, not a promise.
